turn_text: It was a meeting that Mike invited me to, as you said, he said Sidney Powell would be there and she was. And that they just wanted to go over some things with me. It tried to persuade me and anybody else that attended that there should be at least like a 10 day waiting period before the election would be certified. That was a premise of it. And that was always sort of Mike's point and remains to this day, actually. Cynthia Lamas attended it with me, or attended it. I was there. She didn't come with me. And Senator Johnson attended on video. And one of the things I said prior to going into the meeting, I said, look, I'm happy to listen. First of all, Mike's a close friend, and I would do it for him, regardless. Second of all, I said, I do hope, though, that we're going to talk about something other than theories. In other words, for example, there were claims being made at the time, and I think still, that something like 8,000 people in a particular area of Nevada voted that were dead, or several thousands in several places. And I said, I don't, I just want to see the list of those people. Just bring me you know, 8,000 names of dead people who voted. And whatever information is, you know, you can provide so that I can go back and see if they're real. Did they really do that? Things like that. So when I got there, Chris came with me. Cynthia was there. I had a couple of staff people there, including our general counsel. Cynthia had, I think her chief of staff was there. And Rob, or Ron Johnson was on, like I said, Zoom or something. And then just a whole bunch of other people just kept coming. And pretty soon there were, as you said, at least a couple of dozen people in that conference room that was better suited for a dozen probably. But that's neither here nor there. There was even another room in the suite where there were a lot of other people. Mike didn't know most of them. And we had a, I don't know, 90 minute discussion about why this should be delayed by 10 days or so. And we all ask pretty pertinent questions and no evidence was ever presented as to why we shouldn't certify two days later. And it was fairly unimpressive. I mean, that's sort of the thrust of it. Now, these all these other people had other ideas besides you know, dead people having voted, which was like I said, my main interest was I wanted to see real evidence that there was this fraud going on that people are talking about. And of course, I think it was two days later, you did in fact vote to affirm the election result. And I, have you ever seen any evidence through today to this date that would, you know, give a compelling argument for, you know, Biden not being president? No, I have not, and I've been pretty open about that. I mean, in fact, even, I don't know if it was later that day of the fourth or at least by the fifth, because a lot of North Dakotans weren't in town. And I met with them, as you might recall, out in the capital lawn, there was a pretty famous picture of them praying over me in the New York Times. I think a picture that I think occurred about three more times after that, actually. So I announced my intention, at least January 5th, if not 4th, that I just couldn't see a constitutional authority, not to vote against the certification. There's just nothing in the plain reading of the Constitution that would even allow that. With regard to your question, though, why have I ever seen any evidence, I think there's lots of evidence that raises the question of security of our elections. But that's a separate question. And this is why I applaud the efforts of many legislatures around the country to try to provide greater security for our elections. And I think it's also pretty clear that the pandemic and access to voting was a rather special circumstances in the 2020 election that provided for a lot of states, not by legislation, but sort of by executive decisions, administrative decisions, loosen their election laws, particularly the use of ballot harvesting. the waving of the expansion of vote by mail, no excuse vote by mail. And a lot of these things seem to proper, at least appropriate, I shouldn't say proper, seem to appropriate to, I think a lot of people, given again the fact that people didn't want to crowd into small spaces on one day and expose themselves and others to a pandemic, that we didn't know a whole lot about that. That was sort of the rationale for that, although there was, you know, there was plenty of concern raised that if we, if we, if various states or if all states were to loosen their border security regulations and laws that you are opening the door to. potential fraud because I think it's pretty obvious that it's easier to vote by mail fraudulently or have somebody else deliver your ballots for you in large numbers than showing up and proving you are used here. As you know, North Dakota has long been a big vote-by-mail state in rural counties that don't even vote in person. And yes, indeed, anybody who wanted to could vote by mail in that election. And I'm not aware of any irregularities or any problems in North Dakota by voting. I think part of that, though, I think part of that, Patrick, is that we have We have auditors and clerks and election workers that know every name that comes across their table and it comes across their desk. But that's not to say we shouldn't be really, really certain. It provides some further safeguards to evidence that you are who you say you are. And all that can be done and is being done. As an aside, it's just a voter. I love the convenience of voting by mail. Of course, I'm working that day anyway. I know. Senator, perhaps we could talk a little bit about this memo and it's my understanding, the Washington Post has reported that after you attended this meeting that we were talking about, Mike D'Alrasso from Virginia sent you, most of emailed, a very interesting memo that was advocating the use of a national security agency, and I believe Defense, Department of Defense, military intelligence to basically scan raw electronic communications to see if they could find proof of claims that some foreign powers, including China and Venezuela, were intervening in the election in a way to benefit Biden. give him the election victory. I mean, as far as I know, the NSA can't do any domestic spying. Of course, that's the theory. Yeah, that's involved. Yeah. And it done a lot of it. But yeah. Right. This would, I guess, presumably focused on these foreign powers. So it might have been within their charter anyway. What did you think of that? And was this theory, this proposal discussed at the meeting at all? Oh boy, yeah, sure was. It sure was. And of course, I just have fundamental philosophically American level disagree with it, disagree with the idea that the NSA ought to do that, even if they have it within their charter. And we've been trying to do a lot, at least a couple of times, major things that we've done to restrict the NSA's access to domestic data under the Patriot Act. So I was never a big advocate of it. as a recall and remembering none of this stuff was very impressive to me at the time so I didn't really spend a lot of time worrying about it when Josh Dossy the reporter at the Washington Post called me about it. I was hard pressed even find any of that information but I was able to I eventually was able to go deep into the archives of my own electronic communications to find some of it. I think he'd already seen it. He already knew of its existence, which is why he called me. But for comment, I say it's both similar to what you're doing. But none of it was very impressive to me. So I don't, what they really wanted me to do. And when I say they, not Michael and Dell or even, I don't even remember anybody other than like this Mr. Del Rosso and a couple of the other people in more in the intelligence community. They wanted me to prevail upon the president himself and or the vice president to to do this and and that was of course hand in hand with delaying the election by a few days so that they could do a broader or a deeper dive into finding this now. They were of the belief that that Venezuela, a place like Venezuela and maybe China. Others were trying to infiltrate our elections and manipulate them. I think that's pretty clear that places like China, Russia, they're pretty famous for that. And I don't know that I think there's even evidence that they try to interfere with our elections by trying to persuade through social media and other news and things like that. but to actually infiltrate the election process itself, that I've not seen evidence of. But they were of the view that that had happened and the NSA could prove that. They wanted me to bring this directly to the president. But here's what's interesting. It's always interested me at the time. Remembering that I said, Sidney Powell was in the room? She was the president's attorney. I mean, I said, how do I have better access to Donald Trump than you know then Sidney Powell and so I did nothing with it. I mean quite honestly Patrick I did nothing obviously and by the way neither did the president as we know at the end of all of this this very long story in the Washington Post it just the end of it was Some people with, you know, extreme ideas wanted an extreme action that the president didn't do, you know, yay. It worked. Now, you've mentioned, you know, you've made clear that Sidney Paul was at this meeting. Is she one of the presenters, or was she really just listening? Yeah. Actually, that's interesting to ask that question, because she wasn't. In fact, I was sort of surprised at how little she did say at the meeting. I think she was more interested in in the gathering of all these people, and probably is learning as I was along the way in these last couple of days prior to these last really hours prior to the vote itself to, you know, obviously to certify the election. So again, it was a lot of effort that went nowhere, quite honestly. Yes, she did. But no, Sydney really did not say very much. I remember to ask her, though, I said, but what under what authority? Because I was genuinely curious, Pat. I was under what authority, constitutional authority with the president or the vice president, even do any of this, including, by the way, not certifying an election that has been certified by 50 different secretaries of state and election boards. And, you know, there were absolutely not a single alternative slate of electors that we could have even voted for. And she, I think they said, well, under the guise of national security or something. But this was clearly not something she, I shouldn't say it wasn't clearly. She just didn't say very much about it. The Washington Post characterized these claims as fantastical. And I don't know, I find myself thinking of this as really kind of a hair-brained scheme. But I just wonder if they meant to say hair-brained scheme, but they only had so many call them inches. I don't know. I'm asking you to characterize it. Was it just really off the wall? In your view, you've said that you didn't find a persuasive thing. Well, yeah. Patrick, I don't. I don't know. First of all, it was so wonky that it's one of those things like I wouldn't even dare judge. You know how off the wall it was because it would require just a whole bunch more information. This is why at the heart of it all for a simple guy from Kindred, just show me just show me a thousand names of dead people in their addresses that voted so I can go look up the thousand dead people and see if they actually did vote or if it was their cousin or their father or their junior. That's how it boiled down to me. By the way, even if something did present itself, it still was clear to me that I didn't have the authority to overturn an election as a United States Senator on January 6. That's not what the law says, it's not what the Constitution says. So for me, I was trying to boil it down. I'm kind of famous for simplifying complicated things. sometimes because I don't understand the complication. So please make it simple. But so to judge it, to judge the level of seriousness of the effort, I really wasn't. That really wasn't my thing necessarily. But I mean, here I am sitting with people that literally still work in the intelligence community of the United States government and some of them who previously did. You know, it's a little bit like me. It's a little bit like me telling, you know, an engineer that the building they built is, you know, the building that they're designing is far fetched. Yes. Now, of course, I know there's. There seems to be some bipartisan support. I don't know how deep. And of course, the devil's in the details, but there seems to be some support of amending the Electoral College Act to clarify these sort of things. So it's clear that the vice president's role is strictly ministerial. And to try to prevent this sort of thing in the future. And of course, this could be of concern to either party if the opposition tried something similar in the future. should we be looking at clarifying this law and just making it crystal clear so that, you know, this kind of doesn't happen again? Well, it's sort of interesting, Patrick, because, you know, Donald Trump has seized on that movement, and I say movement, I don't know how much of a movement is, but you're right, there are some Republicans and Democrats looking at the electoral contact. I think Mitch McConnell has actually encouraged that. to try and do exactly as you said, clarify what the law is. Remembering that there's the law and then there is the Constitution itself. And he sees that by saying, see, I was right all along. Now they have to change the law because the vice president does in fact have this other authority I said he has. And clarifying it is not changing it. And I think the president, well, let's just say that President Trump at least has a plausible argument when we are trying to clarify something that we say is already clear. I've never been a big fan of clarifying things that are already clear because it can be seen as too much meddling. But every now and then, as I said to you a little bit ago, I like to simplify complicated things and maybe a clarification has some value. But it does raise the question of why isn't it clear already? I believe the clear reading of the Constitution is just that, a clear reading of the Constitution. The Constitution itself isn't very complicated. And the articles that relate to the Congress' role and the Vice President's role in certifying elections is not particularly complicated. I remember reading it directly to the North Dakotans that, you know, that pilgrims to Washington, D.C. for January 6. multiple times I reread and I kept saying show me in this document the Constitution of the United States where I have the authority to overturn someone else's election. And by the way, if I do, Tell me why somebody from New York shouldn't overturn North Dakota's if they don't like the way we vote. It's a pretty fundamental question, Patrick. And I think the more that we argue on the foundation, which is the Constitution, rather than a clarification of it in law, I think that the firmer we are in saying, Congress just does not have this authority that you say they have. I know you're busy. I appreciate your time. I'd love that you think I'm so busy. I'm just left with the worry that, well, I think polls would indicate this, that members of both parties are very distrustful now in elections. And I just think this is very worrisome to our democratic system. If we can't agree on something as basic as who got more votes, And, you know, I just, I really worry about where our democracy could be headed. And I wonder if you were worried too. And, you know, how might we fix this? Well, first of all, I'm not overly worried about it. We've had tumultuous times in the past. You know, you and I have seen a couple of pretty tumultuous elections now. You know, one including one where the Supreme Court itself had to intervene in that, of course, being the first George Bush election, the first second George Bush election. And I think what's different about this time was that there was this populist movement that coming together of a big rally and this particular day that led to this very unfortunate and tragic January 6 riot. Some call it an insurrection. I think it would, as an insurrectionist goal, it would be a pretty lame one. But at the end of the day, the Constitution prevailed. It actually prevailed. I went to the inauguration of Joe Biden. I still get asked about it a lot. Is he really the legitimate president? I'm like, you better be because he assigned a couple of bills I've introduced. So it actually prevailed. But to your other point, the divide in the country, the distrust of elections, how does that get fixed? Well, we're having a struggle with that, aren't we? Because as states are fixing their election laws, you know, securing our elections with tighter, not even tighter, it's not, they're not more restrictive. They're just requiring things like voter ID, requiring, you know, the voter ID, I mean, you know, photo IDs to vote, limiting the role of, or at least maintaining that states have the rights to certify their own elections, to police or elections, to create their own election laws that meet the spirit and the letter of the Constitution and federal laws. Nothing very dramatic, nothing very restrictive at all, quite honestly. It only guaranteeing that your vote really does count. and that the federal government, thank goodness the Congress of the United States has prevailed in stopping liberals and the left from wanting to federalize our elections. Like gosh, that'd be the last thing we should do in this country. And so I really do have a lot of respect for and confidence in states to get it right. States like North Dakota as well as other states to get it right and where they don't get it right, that's up to the people in that state to fix it through our incredible exceptional process. One other question if I may from from the headlines. I just saw that the Republican National Committee voted to to censure Representatives Cheney and Kinzinger of course because they're participating in the January 6th investigation and I guess it was a voice vote and the overwhelming voice vote was was a yay and there was a smattering of no is in there according to reports is that something you know we should be doing, is that, do you support that sort of thing? I support the language of the, I support the sentiment, I guess, of the resolution. I think Adam Kinzinger and Liz Cheney shouldn't be participating because they weren't appointed by the Republican leader. And when the Speaker of the House rejects the minority, the minority's members of a committee and replaces them with her members, including majority party members, but not chosen by the party itself. You now have turned the House of Representatives, the People's House into a dictatorship. And I don't think Adam or Liz should have participated. I think it's an illegitimate commission, even to the point now where they, you know, they send these findings of what do they call it a perjury or not perjury, but obstruction of justice or. charges to the Justice Department that are ridiculous because somebody, because their feelings are hurt because Mark Meadows hasn't cooperated as much as he should within the January 6th commission. Just pure silliness, reducing diminishing, frankly, the people's house. And so I think that's wrong. But do I agree with the RNC censoring them? I don't because the reality is, is that the beautiful thing about the House of Representatives and the thing I loved so much about serving in the people's house is it is the people's. It's not the Republican National Committee's House. It's the People's House. The Republican National Committee largely exists for elected presidents. That's why the Republican National Committee chairman is nominated and appointed by the president when your president, when your president's in power and elected by the membership when you don't have a president in your party in power. And the beautiful thing about the House of Representatives is every member, all 435 of them have roughly the same population. That's the, that's where they call it the people's house. They're up for a election every two years. their own constituents get to discipline them. Their job performance is evaluated just a few hundred days after they're sworn into office. And that's the way the phone has created it. That's why it works the best. And I think for the National Party, again, I support their sentiment, but I don't think you ought to be censoring individual members of Congress. I think that's Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, assuming they're running for reelection, have to go to the Republican voters in their congressional districts or in the case of Liz, her whole state and convince them that they're the right person for the job. And that's where that discipline belongs. Well, thank you.

explicit_propositions.text: Mike invited the speaker to a meeting.
Sidney Powell was present at the meeting.
The meeting aimed to persuade attendees to delay election certification by at least ten days.
No evidence was presented during the meeting to justify delaying certification beyond two days.
The speaker requested specific evidence, such as lists of deceased individuals who allegedly voted.
Chris accompanied the speaker to the meeting.
Cynthia Lamas attended the meeting, though not with the speaker.
Senator Johnson joined via video conference.
A total of at least two dozen people attended the meeting in a space designed for about twelve.
Additional attendees gathered in another room within the suite.

assumptions.text: The speaker believes that constitutional authority cannot be exercised by a U.S. Senator to override a state-certified election outcome.
The speaker assumes that credible evidence of widespread election fraud requires verifiable, named records rather than anecdotal or speculative claims.
The speaker trusts that state-level election processes, especially in states like North Dakota, are reliable due to personal oversight and accountability mechanisms.
The speaker considers it fundamentally unjust and dangerous for one branch of government to unilaterally challenge a nationwide election result based on partisan or speculative grounds.
The speaker views the idea of using the NSA for domestic surveillance related to election integrity as constitutionally inappropriate, regardless of legal technicalities.
The speaker believes that political leaders should be held accountable by their constituencies, not by party committees, for participation in investigative bodies.
The speaker assumes that public trust in elections depends on transparency, verifiability, and adherence to constitutional norms.
The speaker believes that changes to election law should reflect existing constitutional clarity rather than perceived ambiguity.
The speaker holds that the legitimacy of democratic institutions ultimately rests on broad societal acceptance of outcomes, not procedural manipulation.
The speaker expects that meaningful reform of election procedures will emerge from state-level actions rather than federal mandates.
